- When sentiment is positive (≥0.5) and model overestimates, reduce forecast by 2–5% to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is negative (≤-0.5) and model underestimates, increase forecast by 2–5% to capture downside risk.
- If recent history shows strong upward trend (e.g., 3+ consecutive rising prices) and model fails to sustain it, add 1–3% lagged momentum to forecast.
- If model peaks sharply after a spike and then drops, reduce forecast by 5–10% in the following 3–5 days to account for mean reversion.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome exceeds model by >10% in 2+ consecutive days, adjust downward by 1–3% per day to reflect overconfidence bias.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “neutral” (0.0) with model consistently overestimating, apply a 3–5% downward correction to avoid false optimism.
- If model forecast is below 70% of recent 18-day average, increase by 1–3% to avoid underestimating upward bias.
- If sentiment is neutral or negative and model is flat, add 1–2% upward bias to account for hidden market sentiment shifts.
